title: The Bro Hug
hook: The hug between men is often a handshake that changed its mind: a grip, a pull, a bump of chests and two slaps on the back, over in a second.
why:
A generation ago, in many places, straight men rarely hugged each other outside sport and funerals. Now the brief, back-slapping embrace between male friends is so common that it has a name. It is a remarkable piece of improvised culture: a way for men to embrace each other while signalling, through its speed, its slaps and its stiffness, that the embrace is comradely and nothing more.

This chapter takes the bro hug seriously. It describes its forms, what the research says about how the form and length of an embrace change its meaning, what the slaps seem to do, what hugs do for the body and mood, how the rules are changing among younger men, how to read the opening and the release so that nobody is hugged who does not want to be, and what to do when a quick hug becomes something more, which happens at funerals and reunions and is one of the most important moments a man can share with a friend.

teach.p:
The bro hug comes in several forms, usually chosen without thought. The commonest begins as a handshake: right hands clasp, held between the chests, and the left arm reaches over the other man's shoulder for a brief pull and a slap or two on the back. The grip between the chests keeps the bodies apart even as they meet.

The A-frame hug leans in from the shoulders while keeping the hips well back, so that the two bodies form the shape of a letter A. The side hug, an arm across the shoulders while both face forward, is common in photographs and at celebrations. The full embrace, chest to chest with both arms around the other man, is the strongest form, and most men reserve it for moments that matter.

Details carry meaning. Heads usually go to the same side, often the left, and a collision of heads is a common source of awkward laughter. The number and force of the slaps vary from two light pats to a series of thumps. And the whole thing is usually brief, a second or two, with a clear ending: a final slap, a step back, a hand that stays on the shoulder for a moment.

The figures here are mid-embrace in the handshake form, right hands still clasped between them, left arms over each other's shoulders. It is a hug and a handshake at once, and that double nature is the point: closeness offered inside a frame that keeps it safe.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's hugs showed no regular forms. The forms described here are widely observed, though their names and their frequency vary between places and generations, and no systematic survey of them exists.

teach.h: Form and length change the meaning.
teach.p:
In 1999 Kory Floyd showed 164 people videos of two men embracing, varying the form of the embrace and how long it lasted. Both mattered. An embrace in which both people took an equal part was read differently from one in which one person did most of the holding, and longer embraces were seen as more intimate and suggested a closer relationship. People also judged how expected or appropriate the embrace was, and those judgments depended on form and duration too.

How long is a typical hug? In 2011 Emese Nagy analysed 188 spontaneous embraces between athletes, coaches and supporters at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, frame by frame. They lasted on average a little over three seconds, and the length did not depend on whether the people were men or women, or on their nationality. Nagy linked this to a broader finding that around three seconds is a basic window in which people experience a moment as one unit.

The bro hug is typically shorter than that, often under two seconds, which is part of how it keeps its comradely frame. A hug that lasts three seconds or more begins to say something more: grief, relief, reunion, love. Both men usually know this, which is why the length of a hug between men is so closely watched, and why holding on is such a strong signal.

The figures here are in a full embrace, chests close, one arm over the shoulder and one around the back. Held for a second, it is a greeting. Held for ten, it is something else entirely.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the form and length of a hug made no difference to how observers read it. Floyd found that they did, though with staged videos rather than real embraces, and Nagy's average comes from one kind of emotional occasion.

teach.p:
The slaps on the back are the signature of the bro hug, and they have not been studied directly, so what follows is interpretation rather than finding. They seem to do several jobs at once. They set a rhythm, so that the hug has a beginning, a middle and an end that both men can follow. They add vigour, turning an embrace into something closer to a physical greeting between teammates. And they signal the end: the second or third slap usually means time to let go.

Many people also read the slaps as a frame that keeps the hug comradely, a way of embracing that says this is friendship, not anything more. Whether or not that was ever their purpose, they work as a shared code. Two men who both slap know that they are doing the same kind of hug.

The slaps can carry other messages too. Very hard thumps can be a quiet contest, a display of strength that turns the embrace into a test. A single slap, or none, often signals a softer, more serious hug. And slaps that continue while the other man is holding on, as if to hurry him, can feel like a refusal of what he is offering.

Read the slaps the way you would read a handshake's grip. Match their force and number. Soften them when the moment is serious. And when a man holds on, stop slapping. The figures here stand side by side, arms across each other's shoulders, hands resting flat. Not every embrace between men needs a percussion section.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if back slaps carried no meaning at all, or the same meaning in every hug. They have not been studied directly, so this block offers an interpretation to test against your own experience rather than a result.

teach.h: What hugs do for the body.
teach.p:
Hugs are not only symbols. In a study published in 2015, Sheldon Cohen, Denise Janicki-Deverts and their colleagues asked about 400 healthy adults each evening for two weeks whether they had been in conflict with anyone and whether they had been hugged. Then they exposed them to a common cold virus under quarantine. Conflict raised the risk of infection, but less so for people who felt well supported, and hugs accounted for about a third of that protective effect. Among those who became infected, people who had been hugged more often had less severe symptoms.

In a follow-up published in 2018, Michael Murphy, Janicki-Deverts and Cohen looked at mood in the same kind of data. On days when people had a conflict, being hugged was associated with a smaller drop in good mood and a smaller rise in bad mood. The association was the same for men as for women.

These studies measured hugs rather than assigning them, so they cannot prove that hugs caused the benefits; hugs may simply mark relationships that are supportive in other ways. The researchers were also careful to say that a hug from a boss or a stranger may not help at all. But the findings fit the chapter on touch in Part I: welcome touch from people we trust seems to do the body good, and men are not exempt.

The figures here hold each other in a full embrace. The evidence suggests that, between people who want it, this is not a sentimental gesture but a small act of care with measurable effects.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people who were hugged more fared no better after conflict or infection. The studies found that they did, but the data are correlational, so hugs may be a sign of support rather than its cause.

teach.p:
The bro hug's own history shows how fast rules about men's touch can change. The sociologists Eric Anderson and Mark McCormack, whose work on homohysteria was described in the previous chapter, interviewed 40 male student athletes at a British university in a study published in 2015. Thirty-seven of them described cuddling with close male friends, lying together on a bed or a sofa, and most saw nothing unusual in it.

This was a small, particular group, and it would be wrong to treat it as a picture of all young men. But it fits what many people notice: younger men in many places hug more, longer and with less stiffness than their fathers did, and the bro hug, which once marked a boundary, is for some of them simply a hug.

At the same time, the old rules are alive in many families, workplaces, sports clubs and communities. A man may hug his friends freely and still freeze when his father opens his arms. The same embrace that is ordinary in a university changing room may be risky in a different town. Culture, religion and class all shape what is allowed, and the chapters of Part V return to them.

The figures here stand together from behind, one with an arm across the other's shoulders while he bows his head. Whether two men can stand like this without comment depends on where they are and who is watching. That is worth remembering both when you offer closeness and when you judge it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's hugging habits had stayed the same across generations. Anderson and McCormack's work suggests change, but it is based on small, particular groups, and the pace of change differs widely between places.

teach.h: Read the opening and the release.
teach.p:
Because men's hugs are negotiated in a second, reading the opening matters. The chapter on greetings described the signs: arms lifting from the sides, a step that keeps coming, a handshake that turns into a pull. When you want to offer a hug, offer it in a way that can be declined: start with a handshake and let a slight pull show what you would welcome, so that the other man can stay at the handshake without embarrassment.

Not every man hugs, and the reasons deserve respect. Some autistic men find hugs overwhelming. Some men who have been hurt find being held frightening, as the chapter on trauma described. Some faiths limit touch, which Part V discusses. Some men simply do not like it. Watch for a locked elbow on the handshake, a body that stiffens, hips kept far back in an A-frame, a step away. Each says not today, and should be accepted at once.

The release matters as much as the opening. In a quick hug, the slaps and a step back mark the end, and both men let go at about the same moment. If you are still holding when the other man has let go, release immediately. If he is still holding when you are ready to stop, that is a different situation, and the next block deals with it.

The figures here shake hands. A handshake is always available as the place to stop. Offering a hug from there, rather than launching into one, is the most reliable way to make sure that every hug you give is wanted.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men who did not want to be hugged showed no signs of it. Most do show signs, though some freeze rather than resist, which is why offering a hug in a way that can be declined matters more than reading the signs alone.

teach.h: When the hug becomes something more.
teach.p:
At a funeral, a hospital, a reunion after years apart or the news of a death, a man may go into a quick hug and not come out of it. He holds on. His breathing changes. He may begin to cry, often silently, his face hidden in your shoulder where nobody can see it. For many men, this is one of the very few places they will ever cry in front of another man.

What helps is simple and difficult. Stop the slaps. Let your hand rest flat on his back, still, or move it slowly. Stay where you are. Do not speak unless something short and true comes to you, such as “I've got you” or “I know.” Let him decide when it ends, and when he steps back, let him wipe his face without comment.

Afterwards, do not joke about it, and do not tell anyone else what happened. Most men will not mention it again. Some will, years later, and say that it was the moment they finally let go. The chapter on mourning together, at the end of this part, returns to these moments.

The figures here stand side by side from behind, one arm across the other's shoulders, his head bowed. Sometimes the hug comes after, and sometimes this is all that is possible. Either way, the rule is the same: stay, be still, and let him set the length. A man who has been held like that by a friend tends to remember it for the rest of his life.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men who held on in a hug wanted to be released quickly or distracted. Most accounts suggest the opposite, but people differ, so watch for signs that he wants to step back, and let him.
teach.pullQuote: When a man holds on, stop the slaps. Stay still, and let him set the length.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Pulling him in when he offered a handshake
poseGallery.annotation: Start from the greeting he offers. A slight pull lets him choose a hug without your forcing one.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Hugging a man who is leaning away
poseGallery.annotation: Hips back, elbow locked, body turning: he is saying not today. A fist bump or a nod keeps the warmth without the hug.

poseGallery.doCaption: Staying still while he holds on
poseGallery.dontCaption: Slapping and releasing while he holds on
poseGallery.annotation: When a man holds on, the slaps should stop. Let your hand rest on his back and let him decide when it ends.

caseStudy:
Luke, twenty-nine, has two close friends from university, and he greets them in completely different ways. With Sam, it is always the same: a handshake pulled into a half hug, two slaps, a step back and a grin. With Dev, who is autistic and has said that hugs are too much for him, it is a fist bump, and has been for years.

In March, Sam's father dies suddenly. At the funeral, Sam comes over to Luke after the service. Luke goes into the usual greeting, hand out, pull, and his left hand rises for the first slap. But Sam does not step back. He holds on, and Luke feels his breath catch against his shoulder.

Luke's hand stops in the air. He has a half-second of panic, and then he lets his hand come down flat on Sam's back, and stays still. He says nothing. He can feel Sam shaking. Around them, people carry on talking. Luke looks at the wall over Sam's shoulder and waits.

It lasts perhaps twenty seconds. Then Sam steps back, rubs his face with the heel of his hand, and says, “Cheers, mate.” Luke nods. Dev, who has been standing a little way off, comes over and bumps Sam's fist, and Sam laughs for the first time that day.

Neither Sam nor Luke mentions the hug again for two years. Then, at Luke's wedding, Sam says in his speech that the best thing anyone did for him that year was to stand still in a church hall and let him cry. He does not say who.
observe: Notice the forms of hug you see between men this week: handshake pull-in, A-frame, side hug, full embrace.
Notice how long men's hugs last, and what happens when one lasts longer than usual.
Notice the slaps: how many, how hard, and whether they change with the occasion.
Notice a man who does not hug, and how other men adjust to him, or fail to.

drills.name: Hug Census
steps: List the men you hug, or who hug you, and the form each hug usually takes.
Note how long each usually lasts and how many slaps it includes.
Mark any man you would like to hug and do not, or who hugs you when you would rather he did not.
Write one sentence about what the list shows about your relationships.

drills.name: The Declinable Offer
steps: Practise, with a willing friend who knows what you are doing, offering a hug from a handshake with a slight pull.
Ask him to decline it sometimes by keeping his elbow firm.
Practise letting go at once when he declines, with no change in your expression.
Swap roles, so that you feel how easy, or hard, it is to decline.

drills.name: Count to Three
steps: Over the next week, notice the length of the hugs you give and receive.
In one hug with someone close, let it last a full three seconds rather than one.
Notice how it feels, and how the other person responds.
Write a few lines about the difference.

drills.name: The Still Hand
steps: Imagine a friend holding on to you in a hug at a funeral.
Write down what you would do with your hands, your breath and your voice.
Write the one short sentence you might say, or decide to say nothing.
Practise, alone, letting a slapping hand come to rest and stay still.
Write down how you would behave afterwards, so that he does not feel exposed.

quiz.q: A friend says that hugs are something women need and men can do without. What does the research described in this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; studies find that hugs do nothing at all for men
On conflict days, hugs went with less mood change in men and women alike
Hugs help men more than women, because men are hugged less often
He is right; hugs only matter between romantic partners anyway
quiz.explain: Murphy and colleagues found that on days with conflict, being hugged was associated with a smaller drop in good mood and a smaller rise in bad mood, with no difference between men and women. The data are correlational, but they give no support to the idea that men do not benefit.

quiz.q: What did Nagy find when she analysed embraces at the 2008 Olympics?
options: Men's hugs were far shorter than women's hugs at the Games
Hugs lasted about a minute when athletes had won a medal
Hugs lasted a little over three seconds on average, whoever was hugging
Hug length depended mainly on the nationality of the athletes
quiz.explain: The average embrace lasted a little over three seconds, and length did not depend on gender pairing or nationality. The bro hug's usual brevity is part of how it keeps its comradely frame.

quiz.q: What did Floyd's 1999 study of filmed embraces show?
options: The form and length of a hug changed how intimate observers judged it
Observers could not tell the difference between any two embraces
Only the age of the people hugging affected how the hug was judged
Longer hugs were always judged as less intimate than short ones
quiz.explain: Both the form of the embrace and its duration influenced how expected, how intimate and how appropriate it seemed, and what relationship observers inferred. Length and shape are part of a hug's message.

quiz.q: At his father's funeral, your friend goes into the usual quick hug and then holds on, his breathing uneven. What fits this chapter best?
options: Give two firm slaps on the back, so that he can pull himself together
Step back gently and ask him whether he would like to get some air
Say something light to break the tension for both of you
Stop slapping, rest your hand flat, stay still, and let him end it
quiz.explain: When a man holds on, he is not doing a quick hug any more. Stillness, a flat hand and patience let him use the moment; slaps and jokes push him back behind the frame.

quiz.q: What did Cohen and colleagues find about hugs and the common cold?
options: Hugs spread colds, so people who hugged more fell ill more often
Hugs explained about a third of the protective effect of support
Hugs had no link with infection once people were exposed to the virus
Only hugs from romantic partners were linked with any protection
quiz.explain: Conflict raised infection risk less among well-supported people, and hugs accounted for about a third of that protective effect. Among infected people, more frequent hugs went with milder symptoms, though the data are correlational.

quiz.q: At a leaving party, a colleague who never hugs offers you a handshake with his elbow firmly locked. You are a hugger. What should you do?
options: Pull him into a hug anyway, since it is a special occasion
Shake his hand warmly and add your thanks in words instead
Refuse the handshake and wait for him to offer you something warmer
Clap him hard on the shoulder so that he knows you care
quiz.explain: A locked elbow on a handshake is a clear sign that he does not want to be pulled closer. Match the greeting he offers and put the warmth into your words.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific hug with another man that you remember: one that felt good, one that went wrong, or one that became something more than a greeting. Describe its form, how long it lasted, what your hands did, and how it ended. What did it say about the relationship? Then think of a man in your life you would like to embrace differently, more or less, and describe what you would change and how you would make it easy for him to decline.
reflection.guidance: Be concrete about the movements: the grip, the pull, the slaps, the length, who let go first. If you have never been hugged by a man in a way that mattered, that is worth writing about too. Consider whether there is a man in your life, perhaps your father or a son, for whom a slightly longer hug would say something you have not said.

failureMode: The first failure is to hug a man who did not want to be hugged: pulling him in from a handshake he offered, or ignoring a locked elbow, stiffening or a step back. The second is to treat the bro hug's rules as fixed, missing both how fast they are changing among younger men and how strongly they still hold in other places. The third is to slap, joke or let go when a man holds on, pushing him back behind the frame at the one moment he stepped out of it. The fourth is to tell others about a hug in which a man cried. And the fifth is to dismiss hugs as something men do not need, when the evidence suggests that welcome touch from trusted people helps men's bodies and moods as much as anyone's.

watch.title: I Love You, Man: Trailer
watch.notice: A man with no close male friends sets out to make one. Watch the awkward greetings, the hugs that do not quite work, and how much male friendship is negotiated through the body.

reviewPrompt: This week, read the opening of every hug you are offered, match it, and in one hug with someone close, let it last a full three seconds.
